transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-28
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Brooks (Acme Head of Eng), Priya Nair (SRE), Sam Ortiz (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text generation basics, with emphasis on latency vs cost tradeoffs.
- Live streaming demo showing parameter tuning and retry/fallback patterns.
- Security questions re: data retention, audit logs, and KMS.
- Agreed next steps: send benchmarks, security pack, and propose Dedicated pilot dates.

Topics detected: latency vs cost, streaming params, retry/fallback, SOC2/KMS, Dedicated pilot, batching/caching

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, appreciate you carving out time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Liam on the line is our SE who will run the live bits.
[00:12] Jordan: Hi, Jordan here. Excited to see the demo — we're trying to understand where hosted makes sense versus, like, dedicated pools.
[00:18] Liam: Awesome. Quick agenda: we'll do a short overview of the hosted chat endpoint, run a live stream, show parameter effects on latency and token cost, then cover retry/fallback strategies.
[00:30] Priya: Quick note — our SLO is 200ms P95 for short responses, but we can accept higher for long generations. We also need audit logs for compliance.
[00:40] Maya: Got it. We'll point out where logs and KMS integrations live in the Console.
[00:46] Liam: I'll start the live request now — bear with me, internet— okay sending a streaming chat generate with max_tokens 120 and temperature 0.7.
[01:05] [laughter] Sam: Nice, live demo anxiety.
[01:08] Liam: Alright, you should see a chunked stream arriving in the console output window. This is server-sent events style, small deltas. If you implement via the SDK you get the same streaming frames.
[01:23] Jordan: I see it, looks snappy. What's the typical per-token latency here?
[01:29] Liam: For short completions we're seeing sub-40ms per token on the model variant I'm using — note that's with caching off for the demo. With prefix caching and batching it improves. But this hides the cold start for model warm-up which might add 200-300ms on first request.
[01:45] Priya: And cost — how do we think about cost per generation? Are embeddings charged separately?
[01:50] Maya: Embeddings are billed differently; for chat/text generation billed tokens include prompt + completion. We showed a benchmark spreadsheet — I'll send an updated version that maps tokens to estimated $/request for different model sizes.
[02:08] Jordan: Important — our use case is chat replies for retail customer support: many short messages, occasional long threads. So latency for short replies matters more.
[02:19] Liam: Then you'd tune for smaller max_tokens, possibly lower temperature, and use a smaller model for simple intent classification. Also batching and KV caching for repeated prefixes will drop unit cost a lot.
[02:34] Maya: Quick note on hosted vs dedicated: hosted gives fastest time-to-value, but if you need predictable throughput or strict data isolation, Dedicated pools are the path — reserved GPUs, SLA.
[02:48] Jordan: Any easy switch-over path if we start hosted then move to Dedicated?
[02:53] Liam: Yep — same API surface. You can pin a model version and then route to the Dedicated fleet via a simple config change in the Console; no code changes.
[03:04] [00:03] Sam: When the stream fails mid-generation, what's our recommended client behavior?
[03:08] Liam: Good question. For streaming failures we recommend idempotent request ids and resume logic: either retry the entire call if you can tolerate duplication, or use the session-token resume API pattern. We also provide automatic fallback to a smaller model variant when the primary model is unavailable which keeps the app responsive.
[03:28] Priya: Can you show that fallback?
[03:30] Liam: Yeah — I'll intentionally throttle a request to simulate a capacity failover. Give me 10s.
[03:42] [background murmur — Liam typing]
[03:56] Liam: Simulating now — you should see a short error then a failover to the smaller model, and stream resumes with partial output.
[04:10] Jordan: I see the resume — there's a slight change in tone but it's okay. How do we measure quality regression when that happens?
[04:17] Maya: We recommend keeping a small eval prompt set with pass/fail criteria; Redwood Optimize can run those checks and alert on regression. We'll include the Optimize playbook in the pack.
[04:30] Sam: Question on rate limiting — what happens at scale if many clients are calling concurrently?
[04:35] Liam: Hosted has rate limits per API key; Console exposes token-level metrics so you can see concurrency and hotspots. For bursty workloads we have burst capacity and autoscale policies on Dedicated. Also prefix caching reduces overall upstream calls.
[04:49] Priya: Security — does hosted ever touch plaintext customer data outside our region? We need data residency guarantees.
[04:55] Maya: Hosted region binding is configurable; data never leaves the chosen region for processing, and you can opt for Private deployment if you need full on-prem isolation. We'll share the data residency docs and SOC2 specifics.
[05:07] Jordan: Can you talk briefly about backoff and retry heuristics for the client side?
[05:11] Liam: Sure. Use exponential backoff with jitter and cap retries — we typically recommend 3 retries max for idempotent calls. For streaming you should reconnect with a new request id and either attempt resume or fetch full completion. Also detect specific error codes: 429 for rate limit, 503 for service degraded -> apply longer backoff.
[05:30] Sam: What about idempotency tokens? Do you generate them client-side?
[05:33] Liam: Yes, client should provide idempotency_key for operations where duplicates are bad. For chat generations it's often fine to retry without idempotency but for stateful ops it's important.
[05:47] [10:00 — live demo continues with parameter changes]
[05:50] Liam: I'm going to change max_tokens to 32 and lower temperature to 0.2 and re-run a batch of 5 parallel requests to show throughput characteristics.
[06:03] Jordan: Noted.
[06:05] Liam: Starting now — you'll see the per-request latency and the console's token breakdown. Notice the cost delta because smaller max_tokens reduces average token output and latency correspondingly.
[06:25] Priya: Can you show a chart of P50/P95 over time?
[06:29] Liam: Console -> Observability tab. Pulling up a short window — here, P50 ~ 35ms, P95 ~ 180ms during this test run; the P95 spikes are when batching window waits or cold-start on a scale event.
[06:46] Jordan: Are cold starts avoidable?
[06:49] Liam: Mitigations: keep a warm pool, use dedicated reserved capacity, or schedule warm-up traffic. In hosted we have some warm policies but Dedicated gives more control.
[06:58] Sam: If we wanted to cap spend, can we set hard limits?
[07:02] Maya: Yes, you can set budget alerts and token quotas per key; Console supports per-route limits and token caps.
[07:10] Priya: About logs — can we get full audit logs with user-level traces?
[07:15] Maya: Yes, audit logs with request ids, timestamps, and action do show. For Private deployments you can ship logs to customer-owned S3 or SIEM.
[07:27] Jordan: Any specific customers in retail using this pattern?
[07:30] Maya: We have a couple — anonymized case studies can be shared. I'll include a short one in the follow-up.
[07:36] Liam: Back to retries — I'll demonstrate a simulated 429 scenario and the recommended client backoff.
[07:42] [laptop typing noise]
[07:50] Liam: Throttling simulated — you see 429 returned, client waits exponential jitter and retries, finally succeeds on second retry. We recommend graphing retry counts in your telemetry to spot bad client loops.
[08:08] Sam: Good call.
[08:12] Priya: QA — how deterministic are outputs across model versions? If we roll a model update, do we get regressions?
[08:18] Maya: Model updates can change outputs. Use version pinning for stability and Redwood Optimize's regression checks to gate rollouts. Canary deploys are supported so you can divert 5-10% of traffic first.
[08:31] Jordan: For our timeline — we want a pilot in April. Do you think starting hosted is fine?
[08:37] Maya: Yes, host to iterate quickly, then move to Dedicated when you validate throughput and need isolation. We'll propose dates for a 2-week Dedicated trial in the next email.
[08:47] Liam: One more live example: streaming large multi-paragraph responses — watch how tokenization and chunk size affect latency.
[08:55] [demo streaming — longer text arrives in pacing chunks]
[09:20] Jordan: Looks okay, pacing is smooth.
[09:24] Priya: If a stream connection drops on mobile networks, what's recommended?
[09:28] Liam: Use local buffering and resume strategies. For mobile realtime we often recommend shorter messages and optimistic UI updates combined with eventual reconciliation when full output arrives.
[09:40] Sam: Anything we should change in our prompts to reduce token usage?
[09:44] Liam: Yes — concise prompts, using system-level instructions sparingly, and templating repeated context into stored KV cache reduces prompt tokens. Also trim conversation history intelligently by summarizing older turns.
[09:58] Priya: Encryption at rest and KMS — specifics?
[10:02] Maya: Hosted supports provider-managed keys; for stronger guarantees we support customer-managed KMS keys (bring-your-own) and HSM integrations for Private deployments. We'll include the KMS section in the security pack.
[10:16] Jordan: Any regulatory issues for EU data?
[10:19] Maya: Region binding plus Private deployment options cover EU residency. We'll attach the compliance matrix.
[10:25] [11:00 — the call pivots to pricing and trial specifics]
[10:30] Jordan: Pricing — what ballpark should we expect per 1M short-response tokens?
[10:34] Maya: Depends on model; I'll send ranges in the spreadsheet. For hosted smaller models are cheaper per token; larger models cost more but sometimes reduce overall token count if they produce concise answers.
[10:47] Sam: For the Dedicated pilot — what do we need from our infra team?
[10:51] Liam: We'll need a contact for network setup, VPC peering or private link, and any firewall rules. Also decide on KMS approach if you want customer-managed keys.
[11:02] Priya: I'll coordinate with our infra, that'll be me.
[11:05] Maya: Great — Priya you'll be the point for the pilot.
[11:09] Jordan: Can you recap next steps?
[11:12] Maya: Sure — (1) I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and security pack, (2) Liam will send sample SDK snippets showing streaming resume/fallback, (3) we propose Dedicated pilot windows and will await Priya's availability.
[11:27] Sam: Anything else on monitoring?
[11:30] Liam: Console traces and token-level cost breakdowns are available; we also have webhook hooks to export metrics to your observability stack.
[11:38] Jordan: Great, thanks everyone.
[11:40] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up by EOD with the docs.
[11:45] [meeting ends]
